title.en: Word order, still / yet / already, and even
title.es: Orden de palabras, still / yet / already y even

summary.en: English word order is rigid. The verb and its object stay together (_I like football very much_), place comes before time (_We met at the station at six_), and adverbs such as _always_, _never_ and _probably_ sit before the main verb but after _be_ (_She always arrives early_, _He is never late_). **Still**, **yet** and **already** compare a situation with what we expected, and **even** adds surprise.
summary.es: En inglés no se puede separar el verbo de su complemento: «Me gusta mucho el fútbol» es I like football very much. Y «todavía» y «ya» se traducen por still, yet o already según lo que quieras decir, y cada uno tiene su sitio en la frase.

form: Verb + object first, then manner, place and time: _I'll meet you **at the station** **at six**._
Mid-position adverbs (**always**, **never**, **usually**, **often**, **also**, **just**, **probably**): before the main verb, after **be**, after the first auxiliary
**still**: before the main verb; **yet**: at the end, in questions and negatives; **already**: before the main verb or at the end
**even** goes just before the word it emphasises: _even my boss_, _even in winter_

uses.text: **The object stays next to the verb**: _She speaks **English fluently**._ Not _speaks fluently English_.

note.en: Never put an adverb between a verb and its direct object.
note.es: No se coloca el adverbio entre el verbo y su complemento directo.

uses.text: **Place before time**: _We have lunch **at the canteen** **every day**._
**Frequency and certainty adverbs** go before the main verb but after _be_ and the first auxiliary: _I **usually** walk to work._ _He is **probably** at home._ _They have **never** met._

**Still** = longer than expected: _It's **still** raining._ **Yet** = until now (questions and negatives): _Has she called **yet**?_ _I haven't seen it **yet**._ **Already** = sooner than expected: _The post has **already** arrived._

note.en: _I still haven't heard back_ stresses that it is taking too long.
note.es: «Todavía no» se dice not … yet, o still delante de la negación para expresar impaciencia.

uses.text: **Even** adds surprise: _**Even** the manager was confused._ _She didn't **even** say goodbye._

mistakes.wrong: I like very much this song.
mistakes.right: I like this song very much.

why.en: The object must follow the verb directly; very much goes after it.
why.es: En español separamos verbo y objeto («me gusta mucho esta canción»); en inglés no.

mistakes.wrong: I go every day to the gym.
mistakes.right: I go to the gym every day.

why.en: Place comes before time, and time does not interrupt the verb phrase.
why.es: Primero el lugar y después el tiempo.

mistakes.wrong: I haven't still received the invoice.
mistakes.right: I still haven't received the invoice.

why.en: In negatives, still goes before the auxiliary. Alternatively use yet at the end: _I haven't received the invoice yet._
why.es: «Todavía no he recibido» es I haven't received … yet o I still haven't received.

mistakes.wrong: Always I have breakfast at seven.
mistakes.right: I always have breakfast at seven.

why.en: Frequency adverbs normally go between the subject and the main verb.
why.es: «Siempre desayuno a las siete»: en inglés always va entre el sujeto y el verbo.

examples.en: We're meeting the clients at the hotel on Thursday.
He always gets up before six.
My sister is rarely home before eight.
They have probably missed the last bus.
Is it still snowing in the mountains?
I haven't seen the new office yet.
examples.es: Todavía no he visto la nueva oficina.

examples.en: The tickets have already sold out.
I still haven't heard from the landlord, which is worrying.
Even the experts were surprised by the result.
He didn't even say thank you.

explanation.en: Never goes before the main verb, and the object stays next to the verb.
Yet goes at the end of a negative sentence to mean until now.

practice.prompt: She ___ lives with her parents; she hasn't found a flat of her own.

explanation.en: Still means the situation continues, and it goes before the main verb.

practice.prompt: The test was so easy that ___ the slowest students finished early.

explanation.en: Even adds surprise: you would not expect the slowest students to finish early.
The object (football) must come straight after the verb.
